extracted.intended_audience: general readers, comedy writers/performers, students or researchers seeking an overview of comedic genres
extracted.subtask_description: Provide an overview and defining features of distinct comedic genres (how they produce humor, typical subject matter, delivery style) with notable examples. Useful for identifying, studying, or choosing a comedic style to perform or write in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Insensitive to audience sentiment by igniting criticism and ridicule on subjects like racism, sexism or anything hurtful; differs from blue humor or dark comedy as it inclines more towards being humorous than being offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples listed: Daniel Tosh, Brendon Burns, Anthony Jeselnik, Bill Burr, Sarah Silverman, George Carlin, Frankie Boyle, Roseanne Barr, Jon Stewart, Denis Leary, etc. Implies use of provocation and deliberate antagonism of audience sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Differs from traditional punchline jokes and incorporates forms such as observation, satire, surrealism, slapstick and improvisation; emerged as a counter to establishment entertainment and often disregards established comedic movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable performers: Tony Allen, Alexei Sayle, Dan Harmon, Stewart Lee, Kristen Schaal, Hannah Gadsby, James Acaster. Implies experimental forms, hybrid styles, and rejection of conventional joke structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotal comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Named after the Greek term for anecdote; personal stories that may be true or partly true but embellished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples: Kevin Hart, Louis C.K., John Mulaney, Jim Gaffigan, Hasan Minhaj, Trevor Noah, Tig Notaro, Chris Rock. Emphasizes narrative, personal voice, and story-structure in joke delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect humor derived from the comedian delivering something intentionally not funny, or lacking in intrinsic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples: Andy Kaufman, Norm Macdonald, Tim & Eric, Eric Andre, Will Ferrell. Technique: subvert expectations by withholding punchlines or performing awkward/non-sequiturs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Also called dark comedy; deals with disturbing subjects such as death, drugs, terrorism, rape, and war; sometimes related to horror genres. Often delivered by a disliked character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples: Bill Hicks, Dave Chappelle, Frankie Boyle, Jimmy Carr, Louis C.K., Monty Python, Sacha Baron Cohen. Implies using taboo/disturbing subject matter and ironic detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blue comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically sexual in nature (risqué) and/or using profanity; sometimes uses gender- or race-based humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples: Joan Rivers, Dave Attell, Frankie Boyle, Dave Chappelle, Eddie Murphy, Joe Rogan, Sarah Silverman. Characterized by explicit subject matter and adult-orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burlesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsensical or ridiculous treatment of serious works of art, music, literature or theatre to make a statement, in a humorous and entertaining way; prior knowledge of the subject is required by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Play That Goes Wrong, A Modest Proposal, O Brother, Where Art Thou?. Requires familiarity with original work for full effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Derived from a persona invented by the performer, often stereotypical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable performers: Phyllis Diller, Andy Kaufman, Sacha Baron Cohen, Rowan Atkinson, Sarah Silverman, Eric Bauza. Emphasizes sustained persona, physicality, and role-playing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cringe comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy of embarrassment derived from inappropriate actions or words; popular in television shows and film, but occasionally in stand-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/performers: Ricky Gervais, Larry David, Nathan Fielder; TV shows: The Office, Curb Your Enthusiasm, Peep Show. Uses social awkwardness and second-hand embarrassment as source of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Not strictly a style of comedy, it is telling jokes without a change in facial expression or change of emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples: Steven Wright, Tig Notaro, Bill Murray, Buster Keaton, Jimmy Carr. Technique: neutral delivery contrasted with absurd or provocative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heritage comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedian discusses humorous traits or stereotypes about their own culture or heritage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable performers: Trevor Noah, Russell Peters, Gabriel Iglesias, George Lopez. Involves cultural storytelling and identity-based observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisational comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Largely unplanned routines, often performed live and relying on spontaneous creation and audience interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers/shows: Whose Line Is It Anyway?, Robin Williams, Amy Poehler, Tina Fey, Wayne Brady. Implies quick thinking, games, and ensemble collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inside humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires special knowledge in order to be appreciated by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Firesign Theatre referencing obscure Beatles album details. Use: callbacks, niche references—audience familiarity is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insult comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive insults directed at the audience or other performers, usually in response to audience hecklers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable: Don Rickles, Andrew Dice Clay, Jimmy Carr, Jeff Ross. Technique: savage put-downs, aggressive crowdwork; risk of alienating audience if mishandled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mockumentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody using the conventions of documentary style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: This Is Spinal Tap, The Office, Borat, Parks and Recreation, What We Do in the Shadows. Uses faux-serious presentation and documentary tropes to satirize subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Derived from music with or sometimes without lyrics; uses musical performance as the comedic vehicle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/acts: Weird Al Yankovic, Bo Burnham, Flight of the Conchords, Tom Lehrer, Tenacious D. Combines songwriting, timing, and parody for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Pokes fun at everyday life, often by inflating the importance of trivial things or by observing the silliness of social conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable comedians: Jerry Seinfeld, George Carlin, Jim Gaffigan, John Mulaney. Emphasis on relatability, keen observation, and comedic framing of mundane topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-line joke
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke delivered in a single line. A good one-liner is pithy (concise and meaningful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable performers: Mitch Hedberg, Jimmy Carr, Steven Wright, Rodney Dangerfield. Focus on brevity, word economy, and a tight setup/punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar to slapstick; this form uses physical movement and gestures and is often influenced by clowning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/performers: Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, Jim Carrey, Mr. Bean. Requires timing, choreography, and visual expressiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical jokes (pranking/trolling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor based around tricks played on a person or group, generally causing the victims embarrassment, confusion, discomfort, or irritation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hidden-camera shows, Windy City Heat, The Eric Andre Show; acts: The Jerky Boys. Ethical concerns: consent and harm to the target are considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Relies on ridiculous props, casual jackets or everyday objects used in humorous ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable acts: Carrot Top, Gallagher, Tape Face. Visual gag emphasis, timing with physical objects, and vocal/presentational interplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screwball comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre that emerged in the 1930s characterized by fast-paced, witty dialogue, farcical situations, and romantic storylines often involving a battle of the sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: classic Hollywood screwball films and actors such as Cary Grant. Emphasizes rapid repartee, situational absurdity, and romantic conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shock humor
rubrics_metrics.description: A style that uses shock value to invoke a strong negative emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Howard Stern, Jackass, Eric Andre. Relies on extreme content or actions to elicit reaction; high risk of offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sitcom
rubrics_metrics.description: Television series with scripted dialogue set in a thematic situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Seinfeld, The Office, Friends, Parks and Recreation. Emphasizes recurring characters, situational setups, and episodic joke structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch
rubrics_metrics.description: A short scene on television or standup, similar to the sitcom, practised and typically performed live; sketches sometimes spawn sitcom series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows/performers: Saturday Night Live, Monty Python, Key & Peele. Focus on premise, rapid development, and punchline payoff within a short time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoof / Parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous recreation of a book, film or play, either to pay homage or to ridicule the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Airplane!, Weird Al Yankovic, Mel Brooks. Technique: mimicry, exaggeration of tropes, and intertextual references to source material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreal comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on bizarre juxtapositions, absurd situations, and nonsense logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples: Monty Python, The Mighty Boosh, Tim & Eric, Eric Andre. Uses illogic and dreamlike scenarios to create humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical comedy / Satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Relies on news headlines and current affairs; dates quickly but is popular for late-night talk-variety shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Daily Show, The Onion, John Oliver, Jon Stewart. Requires up-to-date knowledge and often political or social commentary; effectiveness tied to timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventriloquism
rubrics_metrics.description: Involves character comedy; the comedian uses ventriloquy to 'throw' their voice into a dummy or puppet character, typically speaking as the straight man and giving comic lines to the dummy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable ventriloquists: Jeff Dunham, Nina Conti. Technique: voice control, character interplay, and skill in puppet manipulation; can incorporate adult material (blue comedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit / Word play
rubrics_metrics.description: More intellectual forms based on clever, often subtle manipulation of language (though puns can be crude and farcical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples: Oscar Wilde, Groucho Marx, Stephen Fry, Bo Burnham. Emphasizes linguistic cleverness, double meanings, and precise wording.
